sentences.text: Ornithocheirus is a pterosaur genus named for its 'bird hand' appearance, established by Harry Seeley in 1870.
The type species of the genus Ornithocheirus is O. simus, known only from fragmentary jaw tips, where the type specimen is represented only by a broken piece of the upper jaw tip.
The original material of Ornithocheirus simus from England indicates a medium-sized species with a wingspan of 2.5 meters, though specimens referred to this species can reach a wingspan of 5 meters.

Both O. simus and O. mesembrinus had distinctive convex, keeled crests on their snouts, and unlike relatives Anhanguera and Coloborhynchus which had tooth rosettes at jaw tips, Ornithocheirus had straight jaws that tapered to a point with teeth that were almost vertical instead of set at an open angle.

Past estimates suggested Ornithocheirus could have had a wingspan of 40 feet (12.2 meters), though this is now considered exaggerated, while modern estimates suggest a wingspan of 15 to 20 feet (4.5 to 6.1 meters) and Gregory S. Paul estimated a body mass of 20 kilograms.
Even the largest remains of Ornithocheirus are damaged and difficult to interpret due to the fossilization process involving erosion and burial in sand.

Most Ornithocheirus fossils come from the Cambridge Greensand of England, dating to about 110 million years ago, where fragmentary pterosaur fossils were found within the Cambridge Greensand formation.

Additional fossils from the Santana Formation in Brazil, dating between 112 and 108 million years ago, have occasionally been classified as Ornithocheirus or placed in other genera like Tropeognathus.

Seeley described 27 species of Ornithocheirus between 1869 and 1870 based on fragmentary material, Reginald Walter Hooley in 1914 merged Owen's genera Coloborhynchus and Criorhynchus back into Ornithocheirus, and in 2013, researchers Rodrigues and Kellner determined that Ornithocheirus is monotypic, containing only the species O. simus.
An enormous pterosaur identified as Ornithocheirus was featured in an episode of the BBC series Walking with Dinosaurs.
Decomposing pterosaur carcasses floated on the sea surface, losing bones that sank to the ocean floor where they were eventually fossilized.

In 2019, Pêgas et al. classified Ornithocheirus as a basal member of the clade Ornithocheirae, a 2025 phylogenetic analysis identified Thapunngaka as the closest relative of Ornithocheirus, Ornithocheirus belongs to the parent group Ornithocheiroidea, and Ornithocheirus is classified within the class Reptilia.
Ornithocheirus lived during the Early Cretaceous period, specifically from the Hauterivian to the Turonian stages, between 132.6 and 89.8 million years ago.
While some species were once referred to Ornithocheirus from North America, Europe, and South America, O. simus is primarily known from the UK and a possible specimen from Morocco.

The poor preservation of the original material for O. simus has caused long-standing issues with the classification of the genus Ornithocheirus, it is debated whether O. simus and O. mesembrinus are distinct species as the type specimen of O. simus is nearly identical to comparable bones in O. mesembrinus, and it is debated whether the genus Criorhynchus is valid with Unwin rejecting its validity in 2000 despite earlier revivals by other researchers.

In 2000, David Unwin argued that Criorhynchus was invalid and that O. simus was the correct type species, which allowed the revival of the genus Lonchodectes, and David Unwin considered Tropeognathus mesembrinus to be Ornithocheirus mesembrinus in 2003.
